# Clerical review with `rLink_inspect()` {#sec-rlink-inspect}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
source("_people.R")
```

@sec-rlink ends with a table of scored pairs and a threshold. For the
pairs well above the cut and well below it, that is the whole decision.
For the pairs *near* it, it is not a decision at all --- it is a coin
toss dressed up as a number, and on a person linkage those pairs are
where the married names, the nicknames, the twins and the
father-and-son-with-the-same-name live.

`rLink_inspect()` is the step between scoring pairs and believing the
result. It opens the candidates in a browser, lets you move the cut and
see what moves with it, lets you accept or reject individual pairs
against the evidence, and writes **every judgement, with a comment, to an
append-only JSON file** that somebody else can read back, disagree with,
and replay.

That file is the point. An afternoon of expert judgement that exists only
in the analyst's head is not a reproducible linkage; the same afternoon
written down against stable pair identifiers is.

```{r}
#| label: workflow
#| eval: false
pairs <- rLink(hospital, registry, block_1 = ..., compare = ...)
out   <- rLink_inspect(pairs)                       # choose a cut, judge the rest
out                                                 # prints the R to reproduce it
pairs <- apply_decisions(pairs, "rLink_decisions.json")
```

## A worked example {#sec-inspect-example}

Block on the surname code and the **year** of birth, so a wrong day or
month cannot hide a pair, with a second pass on the full date so that a
married name is still reachable. Then score the fields *separately*: a
clerical reviewer needs to see which field disagreed, not one number.

```{r}
#| label: demo-pairs
pairs <- rLink(
    hospital, registry,
    block_1 = list(name_year = list(soundex(surname), format_date(dob, "y")),
                   dob_only  = dob),
    compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                   given   = jaro_winkler(given_name),
                   dob     = date_compare(dob),
                   address = jaro_winkler_tokens(address)),
    keep = c("given_name", "surname", "dob", "sex", "address", "postcode",
             "phone", "email"),
    block_key = FALSE
)
pairs[, c("pair_id", "given_name_1", "given_name_2", "surname_1",
          "surname_2", "surname", "given", "dob", "address")]
```

Fourteen candidates, and no threshold settles them. Look at what is
there:

- `HOS-0006 | REG-0006` --- **JENNIFER TAYLOR** against **JENNIFER
  HARRIS**. Everything agrees except the surname, which scores 0.556. A
  married name, and no comparator will ever say so.
- `HOS-0002 | REG-0002` --- **ROBERT SMITH** against **BOB SMITH**. The
  given name scores 0.5 and the pair is a link anyway.
- `HOS-0011 | REG-0002` --- **ROBERT SMITH** against **BOB SMITH**
  again, but the hospital's *other* Robert Smith: born five months
  earlier, in a different suburb, on a different phone. The two name
  scores are identical to the pair above --- 1.000 and 0.500 --- so on
  names alone these two pairs cannot be told apart, and whichever rule
  accepts one accepts the other.
- `HOS-0004 | REG-0004` --- **WILLIAM HENRY WILLIAMS** against **BILL
  HENRY WILIAMS**: a nickname *and* a typo at once.

A cut on the name scores that accepts the second of those accepts the
third. The evidence that separates them --- a five-month gap in the date
of birth, a different suburb, a different phone --- is all on the
screen, and none of it is in the one number a threshold reads. That is
the problem the rest of this chapter is about.

## Opening the review {#sec-inspect-open}

```{r}
#| label: open
#| eval: false
out <- rLink_inspect(
    pairs,
    threshold = c(surname = 0.92, given = 0.80, dob = 0.90, address = 0.80),
    band      = c(0.75, 0.95),
    reasons   = c("married name", "nickname", "transposed date",
                  "same name, different person"),
    decisions = "cancer_registry_review.json"
)
```

![The review screen. Scores carry a colour gradient --- dark means more
like a match --- the table is grouped into *in scope* and *out of scope*,
and the pane on the right is the pair in
focus.](images/rlink-inspect-review.png){#fig-inspect-review}

Six things on that screen are worth knowing about.

**The header counts everything, not what is on screen.**
`9 of 14 in scope (7 by the cut, 2 forced in, 0 forced out)` breaks the
total into what the threshold gave and what a person overruled, because
those are different kinds of fact and only the second needs defending.
`9 clean 1:1` and `0 contested` say what the scope does to the *records*
--- a record claimed by two links is the failure mode a pair-level
precision number hides.

**Out of scope rows are dimmed, not hidden.** A false negative you cannot
see is a false negative you will not find.

**The pane on the right is the pair.** Compared fields first, each with
the value either file held, the score it earned, and *what differs
between the two values highlighted*. In @fig-inspect-review the whole of
`TAYLOR` and `HARRIS` is lit up, because nothing in them matches; on the
line below, only the `REET` of `140 COLLINS STREET` is, because the rest
survives the abbreviation to `140 COLLINS ST`. One dropped letter reads
very differently from a different word, and the highlighting is what
makes that visible without reading character by character. Then every
other carried column,
because somebody deciding whether two records are one person reads the
address, the phone and the email as well as the fields that happen to
have been scored. This is the single reason to pass a generous `keep` to
`rLink()` when a review is coming.

**Below the fields: the other candidates for the same two records.**
Whether a pair is a link is rarely a question about that pair alone; it
is whether it is the best candidate its records have. Each rival is one
click away, and where there are none the pane says so --- *"No other
candidate for either record"*, which is itself worth knowing, and is
what @fig-inspect-review reports for this pair. For
`HOS-0011 | REG-0002` it would instead list `HOS-0002 | REG-0002`, which
is the entire basis for rejecting it.

**A judgement beats the threshold, both ways.** The cut decides the pairs
nobody looks at. Marking a pair a link brings it into scope *though its
scores failed*; marking one not a link takes it out *though they passed*.
That is what a threshold is for --- a way of not having to look at a
million pairs, not a verdict. In @fig-inspect-review the JENNIFER
TAYLOR / HARRIS pair carries an orange marker down its left edge and the
pane says **judged a link, overriding the cut**.

**The stock `reasons` are bound to the number keys.** `1` files "married
name" as the comment on the pair in focus. Over a few thousand verdicts
that is the difference between comments that get written and comments
that do not.

## Choosing the cut {#sec-inspect-cut}

One slider and one numeric box per score, kept in step, so a cut can be
dragged or typed exactly. Beyond `all` and `any`, a rule can be written
out --- `surname >= 0.9 | (surname >= 0.8 & given >= 0.95)` --- checked
as you type, stored with the threshold, and re-applied by
`apply_decisions()`.

![The threshold sweep, and per-row scope labels with grouping turned
off. Each row of the sweep is a cut-off; clicking one moves that score's
cut there.](images/rlink-inspect-sweep.png){#fig-inspect-sweep}

The **Threshold sweep** panel answers the question a threshold is
actually about. For every candidate cut-off of one score it reports how
many pairs survive, how many records each side links, how many links are
cleanly one-to-one, and how many records end up **contested** --- claimed
by more than one link. You almost never know the truth; you always know
when a cut-off starts producing records that two different people claim.

The same evidence is available at the console, which is where it belongs
for a scripted run:

```{r}
#| label: sweep-console
threshold_sweep(pairs, "surname")[
    , c("threshold", "n_pairs", "n_one_to_one", "n_conflict_1", "n_conflict_2")]
```

Read the `n_conflict_2` column: it is **1 at every cut-off, including
the strictest**. `REG-0002` is claimed by both Robert Smith pairs, and
both score a flat 1.000 on surname, so no cut on this score will ever
separate them --- tightening it only throws away good links while the
conflict survives. The sweep says that without being told the answer,
and what it is saying is *stop moving this slider and go and look.*

**Suggest a cut** reads that sweep and proposes the last cut-off that
buys more clean one-to-one links than it does contested records, and says
so in a sentence. Clicking a row of the sweep table moves that score's
cut there, so the evidence and the control are the same object.

Which score the sweep is about is chosen in the sidebar. That matters:
it is the second and third fields, not the first, where a reviewer has
least idea where the cut belongs.

## Which pairs to look at {#sec-inspect-queue}

A threshold is a way of *not* having to look at every pair. Three
features are about choosing which ones to look at instead.

**The review band** is a range of one score --- `band = c(0.75, 0.95)`
above, or the two boxes in the sidebar --- inside which a cut cannot be
trusted and a person has to look. The header counts the pairs in it, how
many have been judged and how many are left, which is the review's
progress bar. *Show > in the review band, undecided* lists what is left.
The cut still decides any pair nobody gets to.

**The queue** is the `max_pairs` pairs put on screen (20,000 by default),
chosen by `review_order()`. It opens as the pairs nearest the cut --- the
ones a threshold cannot settle --- and **Rebuild the queue** draws it
again around the cut as it now stands, or around the band, or as an audit
sample. Pairs already judged stay in it wherever the cut has gone.

```{r}
#| label: review-order
# The same ordering at the console: the pairs a cut of 0.92 on the surname
# settles least confidently come first, and the settled ones come last.
pairs$pair_id[review_order(pairs$surname, threshold = 0.92)]
```

Note where the married-name pair lands: **last**. It is 0.36 below the
cut, so by distance it is the most settled pair in the file --- and it
is also the one the cut gets most wrong. Distance from a cut is a good
way to find the pairs a threshold cannot settle; it is not a way to find
the pairs a threshold settles *wrongly*. That is what the review band
and the audit sample are for.

**The audit sample** answers the other question a linkage is always
asked: of the pairs the cut lets through *unseen*, how many are wrong?
It is a fixed sample of them --- the ones whose identifiers hash
smallest, so it is the same sample whoever opens the review, and drawing
it does not disturb the random number stream. Judge it and the header
estimates the false-link rate with a 95% interval.

The band and the audit are both filed alongside a recorded threshold,
because *"0.82"* and *"0.82, having looked at everything between 0.75 and
0.95 and found three wrong links in a sample of 200"* are different
claims.

## Judging pairs {#sec-inspect-judge}

Three buttons and a comment box on every row, and the same on the pair
beside the table. Ctrl-click (cmd-click) marks rows, shift-click marks a
range, and the marked set is judged in one action --- which is how a
block of obvious links is dealt with without 200 clicks. Marks follow the
*pair*, not the row position, so they survive sorting, filtering and
paging.

The whole review can be done from the keyboard, which is most of what
makes a few thousand verdicts bearable:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `j` `k`, or the arrows | the next and the previous pair, turning the page at either end |
| `y` `n` | a link, not a link --- then on to the next pair nobody has judged |
| `u` | undecided again |
| `x` | mark or unmark the pair in focus |
| `c` | write a comment (`Esc` to come back) |
| `1` to `9` | file one of the stock `reasons` as the comment |
| `Ctrl+Z` | take the last action back |
| `?` | show this list |

Taking an action back is itself recorded. The log is append-only, and a
verdict reached and then withdrawn is a different history from one never
reached. A comment is saved as it is typed, so closing the tab loses
nothing.

Because an override is a decision somebody has to defend, it is reported
as one rather than folded into the total: the scope cell says **forced
in** or **forced out** where the judgement contradicts the cut and
**confirmed** where it agrees (both visible in @fig-inspect-sweep);
those rows carry a marker down their left edge; the header breaks the
total into what the cut gave and what was forced either way; and
*Show > overriding the cut* lists exactly that set --- which is the page
to re-read before a linkage is signed off.

## What gets written {#sec-inspect-file}

Closing with **Finish and close** returns a `read_decisions()` object, so
`out` holds the whole review. The same file can be read back at any time
by anyone:

```{r}
#| label: write-decisions
# This chapter cannot click anything, so here is the file as it stands the
# moment the review opens: the run recorded, the opening cut recorded, and
# nobody has judged a pair yet. `launch = FALSE` is what makes that
# reproducible -- the file is written either way.
review_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "cancer_registry_review.json")
unlink(c(review_file, paste0(review_file, ".bak")))
invisible(rLink_inspect(
    pairs, decisions = review_file, reviewer = "a.analyst",
    threshold = c(surname = 0.92, given = 0.80, dob = 0.90, address = 0.80),
    band = c(0.75, 0.95), launch = FALSE,
    reasons = c("married name", "nickname", "transposed date",
                "same name, different person")))
```

```{r}
#| label: show-decisions
held <- read_decisions(review_file)
held
```

A `read_decisions()` object holds four things, and each is there for a
different reader:

`$runs` --- one row per review session: who, when, on what data, with
which package and R version, and a fingerprint of the pair set and the
scores. If the data has moved under a set of decisions, this is what
says so.

`$thresholds` --- every cut that was *accepted*, with the note the
reviewer typed, the rule in force, and the effect it had (pairs, clean
one-to-one links, contested records on each side). A threshold with a
reason attached is an audit trail; a threshold in a script is a magic
number.

`$decisions` --- one row per reviewer per pair: the verdict, the comment,
and the scores the pair had *at the moment it was judged*. That last part
matters when the comparators are later changed.

`$disagreements` --- where two reviewers judged the same pair
differently. This is the whole reason the file is append-only: a second
reviewer's session is **added** to it, never written over it. Reopening a
file restores *your own* verdicts and comments, and shows another
reviewer's against each pair without filling them in for you --- a QA
pass that opens pre-answered is not a check.

Printing the object ends with the R needed to reproduce and apply exactly
these decisions, ready to paste into the script.

### Applying them

```{r}
#| label: apply
decided <- apply_decisions(pairs, review_file)
decided[, c("pair_id", "surname", "given", "link", "link_reason")]
```

Nobody judged anything in this file, so every verdict above is the
recorded threshold's --- and it is worth reading as an indictment of
thresholds. Seven of the fourteen are refused, and six of those seven
are true links:

| Pair | Refused on | What it really is |
|---|---|---|
| `HOS-0002 REG-0002` | `given` 0.50 | `ROBERT` / `BOB` --- a nickname |
| `HOS-0003 REG-0003` | `given` 0.42 | `THI MINH` / `MINH` --- a dropped name element |
| `HOS-0004 REG-0004` | `given` 0.73 | `WILLIAM` / `BILL`, and a typo in the surname |
| `HOS-0006 REG-0006` | `surname` 0.56 | `TAYLOR` / `HARRIS` --- a married name |
| `HOS-0009 REG-0009` | `address` 0.48 | they moved |
| `HOS-0013 REG-0012` | `dob` 0.50 | `1946-10-11` / `1946-11-10` --- transposed |
| `HOS-0011 REG-0002` | `dob` 0.03, `address` 0.43, `given` 0.50 | correctly refused: a different Robert Smith |

Every one of the six mistakes has the same shape: a single field
disagrees for a reason that is not evidence against identity, and every
other field agrees. The one correct refusal is right for a good reason
--- two *other* fields, the date of birth and the address, carry
evidence the names do not.

And that is the trap. The obvious fix is to loosen the `given` cut, but
`HOS-0002 | REG-0002` (a link) and `HOS-0011 | REG-0002` (not one) score
**identically** on both name fields --- 1.000 and 0.500. No cut on a
name score can ever accept the first and refuse the second. Separating
them has to come from somewhere else: another field, a weight that
combines them (@sec-inspect-weights), or a person.

`apply_decisions()` resolves the threshold and the per-pair judgements in
the same order the app displayed them: the recorded threshold decides
every pair nobody looked at, and a per-pair verdict overrides it either
way. **The counts on screen are therefore the counts the next run
produces** --- a reviewer can include a pair the cut threw out and watch
the header agree with them.

It adds a `link` column and a `link_reason` saying why each pair is or is
not a link: the threshold, or a named reviewer's verdict.

## Why `pair_id` decides whether any of this survives {#sec-inspect-pairid}

Decisions are filed against `pair_id`. They find their pairs again after
`rLink()` is re-run with different blocking **if and only if** `pair_id`
was built from record identifiers rather than row numbers.

```{r}
#| label: pairid-survives
# The same two files, blocked completely differently
again <- rLink(hospital, registry,
               block_1 = list(list(soundex(given_name), postcode)),
               compare = list(surname = jaro_winkler(surname),
                              given   = jaro_winkler(given_name)),
               keep = character())
c(first_run = nrow(pairs), second_run = nrow(again),
  shared_ids = length(intersect(pairs$pair_id, again$pair_id)),
  married_name_pair_still_named =
      "HOS-0006|REG-0006" %in% intersect(pairs$pair_id, again$pair_id))
```

The second run finds a different, smaller set of candidates, and the
pairs it shares with the first still carry the same names. So the
verdict "married name, this is a link", recorded against
`HOS-0006|REG-0006`, still finds its pair. Row numbers would not have
survived: `index_1` and `index_2` mean whatever the inputs happened to
contain that day.

The app says so itself when it cannot promise this: open it on pairs
whose `pair_id` is a sequence number and a banner appears saying the
decisions will not find their pairs again. If you intend to review a
linkage, give `rLink()` a `pair_id` --- see
@sec-rlink-pairid.

## Weights, and reviewing on one number instead of five {#sec-inspect-weights}

With `rLink_weights()` the cut is on the **match probability** alone, the
field scores become the evidence behind it, and the pair pane also
reports how many bits each field contributed to the weight. For a
linkage with six or eight comparators that is a far easier review: one
slider, and an explanation per pair of where the number came from.

```{r}
#| label: weights
scored <- rLink_weights(pairs)
head(scored[order(-weight),
            c("pair_id", "surname", "given", "dob", "weight", "probability")],
     5)
```

Fourteen pairs is far too few to fit a Fellegi-Sunter model --- every
probability here comes out at 1, which is what overfitting looks like,
and @sec-rlink fits one on 34,000 candidates instead. But the *ordering*
is already saying something true: the married-name pair ranks **first**.
The model has worked out from the data that surname disagreement is
common among matches and that agreement on everything else is rare among
non-matches, which is precisely the judgement a reviewer makes by hand
in @fig-inspect-review.

```{r}
#| label: weights-inspect
#| eval: false
rLink_inspect(scored, threshold = c(probability = 0.9),
              band = c(0.2, 0.95))
```

## Running it without a browser {#sec-inspect-headless}

`launch` defaults to `interactive()`, so the decisions file is still
written --- and an unwritable path still fails loudly --- when the call
is made from a script or a test. With `launch = FALSE` the
`shiny.appobj` comes back invisibly, to be run or inspected later.

```{r}
#| label: headless
built <- rLink_inspect(pairs, decisions = file.path(tempdir(), "qa.json"),
                       launch = FALSE)
class(built)
basename(list.files(tempdir(), pattern = "qa.json$", full.names = TRUE))
```

The file is written as soon as the app is built, with the opening
threshold if one was given, so a bad path is an error now rather than
after an hour of review, and the file records that this data was opened
even if nothing was decided.

## Argument reference

| Argument | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `x` | Candidate pairs: an `rLink()` result, or any frame with `index_1`/`index_2` or `x_index`/`y_index`. |
| `decisions` | Path to the JSON file. Read and appended to when it exists, created when it does not. |
| `reviewer` | Who is reviewing. Defaults to the logged-in user; every decision is attributed to it. |
| `scores` | Score columns to threshold. `NULL` reads them from `attr(x, "compare")`. |
| `threshold` | Named starting cuts, e.g. `c(surname = 0.92)`. Recorded in the file as an accepted threshold. |
| `band` | Review band on the first score: the range a person has to look at. |
| `reasons` | Up to nine stock comments, bound to the number keys. |
| `max_pairs` | Most rows on screen, `20000` by default. Every count is still computed over all pairs. |
| `page_size` | Rows per page, 5 to 1000. |
| `order_by` | `"review"` (nearest the cut first), `"score"`, or `"input"`. |
| `font_size` | Base font in pixels, adjustable in the app. |
| `launch` | Whether to run the app. Defaults to `interactive()`. |

### Limits worth knowing

At most `max_pairs` rows go on screen; the analysis still reads every
pair, and the app says so. reactable draws every row of a page, so
`page_size` is capped at 1000 --- there is deliberately no "show all
rows", because at these sizes it would lock the browser tab rather than
show you anything. The threshold sweep is drawn over at most 200
cut-offs, placed at quantiles of the score once it has more distinct
values than that. Columns are reordered and hidden by dragging them
between the Shown and Hidden lists in the sidebar, because reactable
cannot drag a table header.

The app needs `shiny`, `reactable`, `jsonlite`, `bslib` and `sortable`,
all of which are `Suggests`.

- `review_order()` --- the ordering the queue uses.
